title: Locusts and Darkness: Egypt Is in Ruins
summary: God sends Moses to Pharaoh again, explaining that these signs are also meant to be told to Israel's children and grandchildren. Pharaoh's officials beg him to give in, but he offers to release only the men, and an east wind brings locusts that strip everything the hail left. After a brief confession, Pharaoh hardens again; then three days of darkness cover Egypt while the Israelites have light. Pharaoh's final offer keeps back the flocks, Moses refuses, and Pharaoh throws him out, warning that if he sees his face again he will die.
story: This chapter brings the cycle of nine plagues to its end. Egypt's fields are now bare, its officials are openly against their king, and its sun has gone dark. Pharaoh's bargaining reaches its last stage. He has offered sacrifice inside Egypt (8:25), then a short trip (8:28), and now he offers to let the men go (verse 11) and finally everyone except the livestock (verse 24). Moses accepts no partial release: Israel will go whole, with its children and its flocks, to serve the LORD as he directs. The chapter ends with a break in relations. Pharaoh says he will not see Moses' face again, and Moses agrees. Only one plague remains, and chapter 11 announces it.
historical:
Locust swarms were one of the great terrors of the ancient Near East and still strike parts of Africa and Asia. In its swarming phase the desert locust gathers in vast numbers, rides the wind for long distances, and strips crops and trees of every green thing. The text describes exactly that: an east wind blows all day and all night and brings the locusts from the desert (verse 13), and when God sends a strong wind from the west (literally a sea wind, since the Mediterranean lay to the west), it carries them into the Red Sea (verse 19). The prophet Joel later used a locust invasion as his picture of the day of the LORD, and his description of a day “of darkness and gloom” and an army “such as never was of old” (Joel 2:2) echoes this chapter's locusts and darkness.

Many interpreters connect the darkness with the khamsin, a hot wind off the desert that blows in Egypt in the spring and can fill the air with dust thick enough to blot out the sun for days. If so, the timing fits the approach of the Passover in the spring. As with the other plagues, the text's interest lies in what no natural account supplies: the darkness comes at Moses' gesture, lasts three days, and leaves the Israelites with light where they live (verse 23).
cultural:
The darkness struck at the heart of Egyptian religion. The sun god Re, often joined with Amun as Amun-Re, was among the greatest of Egypt's gods, and one of Pharaoh's official titles was Son of Re. For three days the god whose rising and setting ordered the Egyptian world did not appear, while the enslaved Hebrews had light. The text never names Re, but a first reader could hardly have missed the point.

The negotiations also rest on assumptions an ancient reader would recognize. Pharaoh's sneer in verse 10, “May the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones,” twists a blessing into a mock curse. His offers keep something back as a guarantee: men who leave their wives and children, or families who leave their herds, will have to return. Moses' answer, “not a hoof will be left behind” (verse 26), refuses any leash. His reason is worship. Israel does not yet know what the LORD will require in sacrifice until they arrive, so everything must come. In the royal court, being allowed to see the king's face meant access and favor, so Pharaoh's final words in verse 28 are a formal banishment with a death threat attached.
literary: The chapter completes the three-by-three pattern of the plague cycle: the locusts are announced after Moses goes in to Pharaoh (verse 1), and the darkness comes without warning (verse 21). It opens with a new purpose statement. Earlier plagues were so that Pharaoh and Egypt would know the LORD; now they are also so that “you may tell your children and grandchildren” (verse 2), which turns the plagues into a story for Israel's future. One Hebrew verb, to remain or be left, runs through the chapter. The locusts eat what the hail left (verses 5 and 12, with a close synonym in verse 15), not a single locust remains when the wind drives them away (verse 19), and not a hoof will be left behind when Israel goes (verse 26). Egypt is being emptied while Israel is kept whole. The court turns against its king in verse 7, where the officials ask, “Do you not yet realize that Egypt is in ruins?” The closing exchange is laced with irony. Pharaoh threatens Moses with death if they meet again, but the next death to come will fall on Pharaoh's own house.

outline.t: The officials plead, and Pharaoh offers to release the men
Locusts cover the land, and Pharaoh hardens again
The ninth plague: three days of darkness
Pharaoh's last offer and Moses' banishment

doctrines.note: God tells Moses that these acts are to be told to children and grandchildren (verse 2), and Moses insists that Israel will go to worship “with our young and old” and “with our sons and daughters” (verse 9). Pharaoh would divide families; God claims them whole, and the faith is meant to be handed down within them.

God's question to Pharaoh, “How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?” (verse 3), names the root of his resistance as pride. Pharaoh's sin damages everyone under him; his officials see it (verse 7), but he cannot. Sin in Scripture is not only a private matter; a ruler's pride can ruin a land.

The darkness shows the helplessness of the sun, one of Egypt's greatest gods, before the LORD who made it. In Genesis 1 the sun is simply a light God set in the sky, and here God turns that light off for Egypt and leaves it on for Israel.

words.note: Anah, in the form used here, to humble oneself or be brought low. In verse 3 God asks how long Pharaoh will refuse to humble himself. The same root is used of the affliction Egypt imposed on Israel (1:11-12), so the oppressor who afflicted others is now called to bow himself, and will not.

Saphar, to recount or tell in order. In verse 2 God wants Israel to tell their children and grandchildren what he did in Egypt. The command stands behind Israel's practice of retelling the exodus at Passover, which later Jewish tradition calls the Haggadah, the telling. Faith in the Bible is carried in stories told between generations.

Choshek, darkness. It is the word for the darkness over the deep in Genesis 1:2, before God said let there be light. The ninth plague is a kind of reversal of creation for Egypt, a return to the dark, while God keeps light in the dwellings of his people (verse 23).

Sha'ar, to remain or be left over. It appears four times in the chapter, for what the hail left for the locusts to eat, for the locusts that do not remain, and for the hoof that will not be left behind. The repetition tracks the emptying of Egypt and the wholeness of Israel's departure.

christ: When Jesus was crucified, the Gospels say that darkness came over the land: “From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land” (Mark 15:33). In Egypt, darkness fell as the last sign before the death of the firstborn; at the cross it fell while God's own Son was dying. The Gospels do not cite Exodus 10 at that point, so the connection is an echo that readers have noticed rather than a stated fulfillment, but it fits the New Testament's picture of Jesus' death as the heart of a new exodus. The chapter's contrast between Egypt's darkness and Israel's light also runs into the New Testament's language for salvation. Jesus says, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness” (John 8:12), and Paul writes that God “has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13). The exodus from Egypt became the church's pattern for describing rescue from every kind of darkness.

hard.q: Why should the ordinary people of Egypt suffer for Pharaoh's stubbornness?
hard.a:
The plagues fall on the whole land: fields, animals, homes, and bodies. It is fair to ask why farmers and servants should lose everything because their king would not listen. Several considerations are offered. First, the ancient world assumed a solidarity between a ruler and his people that modern individualism does not, and the officials in verse 7 clearly understand that Pharaoh's choices are ruining them all. Second, Exodus presents the oppression as national, not only royal. Pharaoh “commanded all his people” to throw the Hebrew boys into the Nile (1:22), and the Egyptians “worked the Israelites ruthlessly” (1:13). Third, the plagues came gradually and with warnings, and when a warning offered a way to escape, some Egyptians took it (9:20). Many Egyptians later show favor to Israel (11:3; 12:36).

None of this makes the suffering small, and the text does not pretend it is. What it insists on is that the one responsible for prolonging it was Pharaoh, whose own court begged him to relent. The rest of Scripture also refuses to write Egypt off. Isaiah looks ahead to a day when the LORD will say, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). The God who judged Egypt did not stop intending good for it.

questions: Pharaoh kept offering partial obedience: some of the people, some of the way, without the flocks. Where are you tempted to offer God a negotiated version of what he has asked?
God wants his acts told to children and grandchildren. What story of God's faithfulness would you want the next generation in your family or church to know?
Pharaoh's officials could see that Egypt was in ruins while he could not. What helps a person, or a leader, see what everyone around them already sees?
